name: Lawyer
description: Lawyers advise and represent clients in courts, before agencies and in private dealings — researching the law, drafting documents, negotiating, and arguing cases. In Florida the route runs through a Juris Doctor from an ABA-accredited law school, the Florida Bar Examination and the Multistate Professional Responsibility Examination. ⚠ There is no required or preferred undergraduate major: law-school applicants arrive from every field listed below.
credentialNote: The Florida Bar states the requirements as: a Juris Doctor degree from an AMERICAN BAR ASSOCIATION-ACCREDITED law school, passing the Florida Bar Examination, passing the Multistate Professional Responsibility Examination (MPRE), producing satisfactory evidence of good moral character and fitness, and filing the applications and fees. Educational eligibility sits in Rule 4-13.1 of the Rules of the Supreme Court Relating to Admissions to the Bar. ⚠⚠ NOTHING BEFORE LAW SCHOOL IS A CREDENTIAL. No undergraduate major, minor, certificate or paralegal qualification shortens this route or substitutes for any part of it — which is why the courses below are chosen for the skills they build, not for sounding legal. ⚠ One thing to do EARLY: the Board of Bar Examiners recommends filing a student registration application in your FIRST YEAR of law school — the fee is lower, and you get a preliminary decision on character and fitness while there is still time to deal with anything it raises.
bodyHtml:
There is no pre-law major, and the data is blunt about it

Law schools do not require or prefer a particular undergraduate degree, and the Law School Admission Council’s own applicant figures show it: the fields below account for law-school applicants in wildly different numbers, and the single largest — political science — is still only about one applicant in six. The rest arrive from psychology, criminal justice, English, economics, history, philosophy, sociology, communications, business, accounting and dozens of smaller fields.

⚠⚠ The law-sounding majors are not the advantage they sound like

This is the part worth reading twice. Ranked by mean highest LSAT score, LSAC’s 2018–19 applicant data puts the most obviously legal majors at the bottom and the abstract, reading-and-argument majors at the top:

Highest mean LSATLowest mean LSAT
Economics 159.7Criminal Justice 146.6
Philosophy 157.9Pre-Law 148.5
International Relations 157.4Law 149.2
History 156.8Criminology 149.4
English 155.7Legal Studies 149.8

⚠ LSAC prints a caution with this data, and it is right: “It would be a mistake to infer from them that any one major is better than another in preparing students for the LSAT or, indeed, for law school itself. It is not possible to know whether or not the students whose data are captured here would have performed equally well on the LSAT regardless of their selected major.” The students, not the syllabus, may be what differs.

So do not read the table as a ranking of majors. Read it as a warning against one specific mistake: choosing a major because it has “law” or “justice” in the title, on the assumption that it is the preparation admissions wants. It is not, and the numbers give no support at all to the idea that it helps.

What actually prepares you

The LSAT tests reading comprehension, logical reasoning and argumentative writing, and law school tests the same things harder. That points at coursework rather than at a subject:

  • Formal logic — the one course on this page whose content maps directly onto a section of the admission test.
  • Heavy reading in dense prose, with an argument to reconstruct — philosophy, history, literature, theory-led social science.
  • Writing that takes a position and defends it against the strongest objection, repeatedly, with feedback. Volume matters more than the department.
  • Quantitative literacy. Statistics and economics turn up constantly in modern practice — damages, antitrust, employment discrimination, regulatory work.

Choose the major you will do best in. Law-school admission weighs undergraduate GPA and LSAT heavily, so a subject that holds your attention for four years serves you better than one picked for its name.

⚠ Paralegal studies is a different credential, not a step toward this one

Florida runs a substantial paralegal route — an A.S. at the state colleges using PLA1xxx/PLA2xxx numbers and a BS in Legal Studies at the universities using PLA3xxx/PLA4xxx. It is a real profession and a good one, and it is not a partial law degree. No part of it reduces what Rule 4-13.1 requires. Take paralegal coursework because you want to understand legal work from the inside or want the qualification itself — not on the belief that it counts toward becoming a lawyer.

Timing, which catches people out

Most law schools admit on a rolling basis, so applying early is a real advantage rather than a tidy habit. The Florida Bar’s own guidance is to begin the application process about a year ahead and to submit applications by November or December, ahead of the stated deadlines. Then, once you are in law school, file the student registration in your first year for the reasons in the licensure note above.

cipCodes.note: Political Science and Government — 12,967 applicants, 17.5% of the total and by far the largest single feeder (LSAC, 2018–19).
Psychology — 3,850 applicants, 5.2% (LSAC, 2018–19). The second-largest single major.
Criminal Justice — 3,673 applicants, 5.0% (LSAC, 2018–19). ⚠ Also the lowest mean LSAT of any major in the table; see the note on law-sounding majors.
English — 3,402 applicants, 4.6% (LSAC, 2018–19), and among the stronger performers on the admission test.
Economics — 3,235 applicants, 4.4% (LSAC, 2018–19), and the HIGHEST mean LSAT of the large majors at 159.7.
History — 3,192 applicants, 4.3% (LSAC, 2018–19). Sustained reading and evidence-based argument.
Philosophy — 2,300 applicants, 3.1% (LSAC, 2018–19), second-highest mean LSAT at 157.9.
Finance — 1,683 applicants, 2.3% (LSAC, 2018–19). Common among those heading for corporate, tax and securities practice.
International Relations — 1,223 applicants, 1.7% (LSAC, 2018–19), with a high mean LSAT at 157.4.
Legal Studies (undergraduate, non-professional) — 1,031 applicants, 1.4% (LSAC, 2018–19). ⚠ It is NOT a partial law degree and its mean LSAT is among the lowest.
Accounting — 1,005 applicants, 1.4% (LSAC, 2018–19). The usual route into tax practice.

courses.reason: Introduction to Logic — validity, formal structure and fallacy. The one lower-division course whose content maps directly onto the LSAT’s logical-reasoning section, and onto reading a statute or an opinion closely.
Composition I — the writing gateway everywhere in Florida, and a Gordon Rule course where a C-minus does not count toward the requirement.
courses.variantNote: ⚠ Two ids carry this course. ENC1101 is the form 39 Florida public institutions use; ENC1101C is used by three, at 4 credits rather than 3. The guide currently sits on ENC1101C.

courses.reason: Composition II — argument, sources and research writing. Closer than anything else at this level to what a legal memorandum demands: a position, the evidence for it, and the strongest objection answered.
Introduction to Philosophy — sustained reading of difficult prose with an argument to reconstruct, which is the daily work of law school.
Social and Political Philosophy — justice, rights, liberty and the authority of law, which is the theory the constitutional material later assumes.
American National Government — separation of powers, federalism and the courts’ place among them. The structural map every constitutional law course starts from.
The First Amendment — the constitutional doctrine most likely to be met before law school, and a genuine test of whether close doctrinal reading suits you.
courses.variantNote: ⚠ Taught in POLITICAL SCIENCE at some Florida institutions and in JOURNALISM AND MASS COMMUNICATION at others, and the two are different courses. The political-science version covers all six freedoms with the religion clauses at length; the journalism version concentrates on speech and press, defamation, privacy and shield laws. A pre-law student wants the first. The test: look for the religion clauses on the reading list.

courses.reason: United States History to 1877 — the founding, the Constitution’s drafting and the Civil War amendments, which constitutional argument returns to constantly.
United States History since 1877 — the administrative state, civil rights and the modern regulatory landscape most practice actually operates in.
Principles of Macroeconomics — economics majors post the highest mean LSAT of any large feeder, and the reasoning transfers whatever you major in.
Principles of Microeconomics — incentives, markets and efficiency: the analytical frame behind antitrust, contract, regulation and much of damages.
Statistics — expert evidence, sampling and significance appear in employment discrimination, antitrust and toxic-tort litigation, and few law students arrive able to read them.
courses.variantNote: ⚠ Two ids carry this course. STA2023 is the form 39 Florida public institutions use; STA2023C is used by one. The guide currently sits on STA2023C.

courses.reason: Public Speaking — arguing on your feet under questioning, which is examined in law school and unavoidable in practice.
Crime in America — how the criminal process actually runs, useful background for anyone considering prosecution, defence or public-interest work.
Introduction to Paralegal Studies — an honest look at how legal work is done day to day, and a way to find out early whether the work appeals.
courses.variantNote: ⚠⚠ A DIFFERENT CREDENTIAL, not a step toward this one. Paralegal studies is its own profession with its own qualification; no part of it reduces what Rule 4-13.1 requires for bar admission. Florida also splits the subject by sector — PLA1xxx/PLA2xxx at the state colleges, PLA3xxx/PLA4xxx at the universities — so the same subject is renumbered at upper division and the content is met twice.
